title: Scientists Reverse Coral Bleaching at Record Speed, Offering Hope for Global Reefs
body:
A team of marine biologists has reported the first successful reversal of severe coral bleaching by exposing dying fragments to healthy coral tissue, achieving full recovery in just seven weeks – the fastest turnaround ever recorded. The breakthrough, demonstrated in a controlled laboratory environment, offers a tantalizing glimpse of a possible rescue strategy for reefs worldwide that are under relentless pressure from rising sea temperatures and ocean acidification.

The researchers collected ghost‑white, bleached colonies of the stony coral *Acropora millepora* from a reef that had experienced a recent heatwave. These specimens were on the verge of mortality, having lost the symbiotic algae (zooxanthellae) that provide them with nutrients and colour. In a series of experiments, the team placed the bleached fragments in close proximity to small, healthy “donor” clones of the same species for a brief period of 48 hours. Within that window, microscopic observations revealed a rapid transfer of algal cells and associated microbial communities from the donors to the stressed corals. By the end of the seven‑week monitoring period, the previously bleached samples had regained their vibrant hues, normal growth rates, and photosynthetic efficiency, indicating a full functional recovery.

The phenomenon hinges on a process known as “symbiont shuffling,” wherein corals can acquire new, more tolerant strains of zooxanthellae from neighboring individuals. While the concept has been documented in nature, this study is the first to demonstrate that a short, intentional exposure to healthy tissue can catalyse a complete turnaround even for corals that were thought to be beyond rescue. The researchers attribute the speed of recovery to several factors: the close genetic match between donor and recipient, the controlled temperature and light conditions that minimized additional stress, and the presence of supportive bacterial communities that facilitate algal uptake.

Experts caution, however, that laboratory success does not automatically translate into field applicability. “The controlled environment eliminates many of the variables that reefs face in the wild—fluctuating temperatures, predation, sedimentation, and disease,” said Dr. Lina Ortega, a coral ecologist not involved in the study. She added that scaling the technique would require massive numbers of donor colonies and logistical solutions for delivering them to remote reef sites. Moreover, the long‑term stability of the newly established symbiosis remains unknown; it is unclear whether the rescued corals will retain their resilience when subsequent heat stress events occur.

Nonetheless, the findings inject fresh optimism into a field that has grappled with bleak forecasts. Global coral cover has declined by roughly 30 % over the past three decades, and many scientists have warned that without rapid intervention, entire reef systems could collapse. The new method could complement existing strategies such as selective breeding of heat‑tolerant corals, assisted gene flow, and the deployment of artificial reef structures. By providing a relatively quick “boot‑strap” to restore bleaching‑affected colonies, it may buy critical time for broader conservation measures to take effect.

Looking ahead, the research team plans to test the approach in semi‑natural mesocosms that more closely mimic oceanic conditions, and eventually in situ trials on degraded reef patches. If successful, the technique could become a cornerstone of active reef restoration, offering a pragmatic tool to reverse bleaching episodes that are currently deemed irreversible. While the battle to save the world’s coral reefs is far from over, this rapid‑recovery breakthrough marks a significant step toward turning the tide for some of the planet’s most vulnerable marine ecosystems.
